questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The three-movement structure of To His Coy Mistress
questions.learningObjective: Explain the function of the poem's three movements
questions.stem: The group splits the poem into sections and finds its argument moves in three stages. Explain what each stage does.

answer.exemplar: The first stage establishes the situation and the stakes: if the addressee is coy, then the speaker's time and the addressee's own interests are being wasted, and the poem's whole question turns on whether this delay is worth what it costs. The second stage raises the difficulty, showing that a defence against intrusion takes time to build and that hesitation is not the same as refusal. The third stage resolves the problem by turning delay into advantage, arguing that haste now secures the whole future rather than forfeiting it.

questions.explanation: The explanation must assign a distinct function to each stage, since the poem's force comes from the sequence of them. Treating them as three illustrations of one point removes the movement.
questions.hint: Situation, difficulty, then the turn that solves it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dryden's elegy on John Oldham and its criticism of the dead man
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the elegy handles the faults of its subject
questions.stem: In the revision notes, someone writes that Dryden's elegy praises its subject without qualification. Write the correction they should make.

answer.exemplar: The elegy does not withhold criticism; it is candid about its subject's faults, including the suggestion that carelessness about his health and his habits of excess contributed to his early death. That candour is what makes the praise carry weight, since a commemoration that treated him as faultless would be read as a routine courtesy. The poem's method is to name the failings and then set them against genuine qualities, so that the elegy becomes an argument about how a life should be judged rather than a simple record of grief.

questions.explanation: The correction must name the presence of criticism and connect it to the weight of the praise. The elegy argues about judgement, it does not merely flatter.
questions.hint: The elegy names faults as well as virtues.

answer.exemplar: The two poems show that a shared addressee does not produce a shared poem. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Marvell's To His Coy Mistress and its posthumous printing
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the poem's early history matters
questions.stem: Comparing the first printing with the manuscript tradition, the group asks why the poem's history matters. Write the answer they should give.

answer.exemplar: The poem circulated for years in manuscript, in song and in private copying before it was printed, so its early history is largely one of transmission by hand, which is a different kind of existence from print. When it finally appeared it did so in a volume assembled after the poet's death, containing pieces by several writers, and it reached the public through that context rather than as a single author's new book. The history therefore bears directly on how the poem was read, since for a long time people knew it as a song-like piece circulating among acquaintances before it became a printed text with a stable place in an author's collection.

questions.explanation: The answer must distinguish manuscript circulation from print and show how each shapes the poem's early readers. Print made the poem a public object rather than a shared one.
questions.hint: Manuscript and print are different kinds of existence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dryden's Fables and the Chaucer couplets inside them
questions.learningObjective: Explain the significance of the couplet measure in the retellings
questions.stem: Reading the collection aloud, the group notices that the retelling is in couplets. Write what they should notice about why that matters.

answer.exemplar: The choice of couplets is a modernisation, because the source narratives were written in a lighter measure and the couplet was the fashionable form of the poet's own moment, so the recasting places the old stories in the present of the language. It also has a moral effect, since the plainness of the couplet draws attention to argument and reflection rather than to the raw materials of the original tales. And it changes decorum, because the more elevated verse form resists the bawdy comic matter it is given, so a retelling in this measure cannot repeat everything the source allowed itself.

questions.explanation: The explanation must connect the metrical choice to period, tone and decorum. Noting only that the metre changed leaves out what the change does to the material.
questions.hint: A changed measure changes period, tone and decorum.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Temple, 1633, and the machinery that put it in print
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the printed collection is not a neutral copy
questions.stem: In their answers to last week's questions, the group must explain why the 1633 printing is not a neutral copy of a manuscript. Write the answer.

answer.exemplar: The printing involved decisions of its own, from the choice of type size and the setting of short lines to the way the compiler arranged and divided the poems for the page. Some of the manuscript's arrangement and spelling was altered, and material was adjusted to suit the printed shape, so the printed collection is a version shaped by the needs of print and by the judgement of those who prepared it. This is why the printed text has to be studied as an artefact in its own right, since the differences between manuscript and print are evidence about the process of making a book rather than simply errors to be corrected.

questions.explanation: The answer must show the printing as an active process with decisions of its own, and the differences as evidence rather than errors. That makes the printed book worth studying separately.
questions.hint: Print made choices; the differences are evidence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The three-movement structure of To His Coy Mistress
questions.learningObjective: Argue that the poem's middle movement is necessary
questions.stem: One member objects that the poem's argument is too simple to need three movements. Write the rebuttal the group should accept.

answer.exemplar: The three movements are necessary because the poem has two distinct problems to solve. The first movement does not know what the second one turns out to be, since it has not yet considered that a refusal might be well meant and require preparation, which is a difficulty the opening has quietly ignored. Only when that difficulty is stated can the closing movement do its work of redefining haste, so the poem cannot jump from the opening demand straight to its conclusion without losing the obstacle that makes the conclusion persuasive.

questions.explanation: The rebuttal must show the middle movement introducing a problem the opening had not seen, so that the close has something to solve. That makes the structure more than decorative.
questions.hint: The middle introduces the problem the close solves.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the making of the 1633 printed collection
questions.stem: At the end of the session, the group writes a note on the 1633 collection and the work that made it. Write the note.

answer.exemplar: The collection was put together by a compiler who gathered poems from several hands, and the result was then handed to a university press, whose compositors and type made the book a distinctive object in its own right. Because the setting of short lines and the choice of type sizes were made for print rather than copied from the manuscript, the volume differs in places from the author's own arrangement, and scholars treat those differences as evidence about how the book was made. The printed collection therefore carries two kinds of history at once, the history of the poems' gathering and the history of their production as a printed artefact.

questions.explanation: The note must name both the gathering of material and the production of the printed object. That is what makes the 1633 volume an artefact worth studying in itself.
questions.hint: Gathering and production are two histories in one book.

answer.exemplar: The group should conclude that the two states are not two editions of the same text with the same content, since a scene that carries the poem's comedy and its social satire simply does not exist in the shorter state. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dryden's elegy on John Oldham and its criticism of the dead man
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the elegy handles its subject's faults
questions.stem: During the mock exam, the group must explain how Dryden's elegy handles the dead man's faults. Write the answer.

answer.exemplar: The elegy does not pretend its subject was free of weaknesses, and it treats the naming of them as part of the tribute rather than as a departure from it. One fault in particular is singled out, the suggestion that carelessness about his own health, including his drinking, cut his life short, and the poem presses that point with some severity. The effect is argumentative rather than merely corrective: the elegy is setting out how a talent should be judged and treated, and the faults it names become evidence for its complaint about the conditions in which such men were used and then discarded.

questions.explanation: The answer must connect the naming of faults to the elegy's larger argument about how talent should be judged. The criticism is part of the tribute's method, not a lapse from it.
questions.hint: The faults are evidence for the elegy's argument.

questions.topic: Two different poems both addressed to Celia
questions.learningObjective: Correct the assumption that the two poems are companions

answer.exemplar: The two poems share a name, and the name has probably helped people group them, but nothing in their making shows that they were written as a pair or meant to be read together. Their arguments differ substantially, their forms differ, and their occasions differ, and the reasons each gives for urgency are not the same reasons at all. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Herbert's curtal sonnet and the punctuation that serves as a stave
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of the sonnet's punctuation
questions.stem: The group prepares an answer on the curtal sonnet's punctuation. Write the answer they should give.

answer.exemplar: In the sonnet the poet has deliberately shortened a line and closed it with a full stop where a reader would expect the line to run on, and the effect is to break the poem into two halves at the point where its argument changes direction. The shortened line is a device rather than a defect, and it works with the punctuation to make the shift audible and visible on the page, so that the reader physically registers the turn before the new claim begins. The practice is not isolated either, since comparable breaks appear elsewhere in the same collection, which shows it as a habit of the volume rather than an accident.

questions.explanation: The answer must describe the device's effect on the argument and on the reader's experience of the turn. Calling the break a printing error removes both the effect and the pattern.
questions.hint: The break makes the turn audible on the page.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dryden's elegy on John Oldham and its criticism of the dead man
questions.learningObjective: Explain the structural role of the elegy's attack
questions.stem: The revision group works out why the elegy's attack on the living matters to its structure. Write what they should say.

answer.exemplar: The attack is not an ornament attached to a lament but the poem's way of making its case. Having argued that the dead man's critical writing deserved better than it received, the poet then takes the offensive, and the abuse of the writers who had disparaged him becomes the demonstration of the point: it shows the practice of satire being used as those who attacked it would have used it. The digression also relieves the pressure of grief, so that the poem returns to commemoration with its argument sharpened rather than with its subject merely mourned.

questions.explanation: The explanation must show the attack as the poem's argument in action, not as a diversion. It demonstrates the defence of satire while carrying the elegiac complaint.
questions.hint: The attack demonstrates the poem's argument.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The three-movement structure of To His Coy Mistress
questions.learningObjective: Argue that the poem's movements cannot be merged
questions.stem: The group debates whether the poem's three movements could be run together into one. Write the argument they should settle.

answer.exemplar: They could not, because the middle movement exists to introduce a difficulty that the opening had not anticipated. The opening treats coyness as a simple withholding that the speaker's urgency can correct, and the middle shows that a refusal may be deliberate, that it may have its reasons, and that preparing for it takes time, which is why a request cannot simply be pressed. Only when the poem has confronted that difficulty can the closing movement redefine haste as the way of gaining future time, and removing the middle leaves the closing claim resting on an argument it never made.

questions.explanation: The argument must show that the middle movement is what makes the closing redefinition possible. Merging the parts would remove the poem's answer to its own objection.
questions.hint: The close needs the middle's problem to solve.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Temple, 1633, and the machinery that put it in print
questions.learningObjective: Describe why the printed collection is worth studying as an object
questions.stem: In a revision podcast, the group describes what makes the 1633 collection worth studying as an object. Which description is best?

options.text: It is the earliest printed source for most of the poems, so later editors must follow it.
options.misconception: treats first printing as authoritative in every respect

options.text: It is valuable because the poems are better here than in any later edition of the collection.
options.misconception: claims general superiority without evidence

options.text: It is valuable chiefly for its illustrations, which show how the pages were meant to look.
options.misconception: attributes the book's interest to decoration, not production

options.text: It is valuable because the decisions of gathering and printing are themselves part of what the book is.

questions.explanation: The collection's interest lies partly in a group of poems gathered, arranged and set in type by particular people, whose decisions stay legible in the object. Treating it only as a source loses that.
questions.hint: The making is part of what the book is.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two different poems both addressed to Celia
questions.learningObjective: Assess a claim that the two poems are revisions of one another

stimulus.body: From the seminar: two poems carry the same addressee's name, and one of them is often used as a synonym for the other. A member has written that this is because the two poems are really the same piece in different clothes, one earlier and one revised.

questions.stem: The group must assess that member's claim about the two poems. Which response is best?

options.text: The claim is right, since a repeated addressee indicates an author revising an earlier poem.
options.misconception: treats a shared addressee as evidence of revision

options.text: The claim is wrong, since the poems make different arguments and nothing shows one revised the other.
The claim is right, since a shared addressee is the standard sign of a revision sequence.
options.misconception: asserts a standard convention with no basis in the poems

options.text: The claim is wrong, but only because the second poem is much shorter and brevity proves independence.
options.misconception: proves independence from length, not from the arguments

questions.explanation: A shared addressee is not evidence of revision, and the poems reason differently, so the resemblance in address is naming, not identity. The note should correct the claim from the arguments.
questions.hint: A shared name is not a textual relationship.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dryden's elegy on John Oldham and its criticism of the dead man
questions.learningObjective: Describe the method of the elegy
questions.stem: The study group sets out to describe the elegy's method. Write the description they should prepare.

answer.exemplar: The elegy praises and corrects at the same time, and the corrections are not decorative. It commends the dead man's critical writing and the sharpness of his judgement, then names a serious personal failing, suggesting that his own habits, particularly his disregard for his health, contributed to his early death. It then turns outward to attack the living writers who had attacked him, arguing for satire's value while administering abuse. The result is a portrait that keeps the man inside a larger argument about how writers should be treated and how talent should be judged.

questions.explanation: The description must hold praise, criticism and the outward attack together in one method, and connect them to the poem's larger argument. Listing the sections separately loses the design.
questions.hint: Praise, correction and attack, serving one argument.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The three-movement structure of To His Coy Mistress
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a developing structure from a list of reasons
questions.stem: Before the reading group, a member says the poem's structure is simply a list of reasons. Which description of the structure is best?

options.text: It is a list, since each movement gives a fresh reason and none depends on another.
options.misconception: treats a developing argument as independent points

options.text: It is a list, since the poem ends where it began and adds nothing to the opening.
options.misconception: denies the poem's movement while keeping the form

options.text: It is not a list, since the argument is carried entirely by the imagery and the prose is filler.
options.misconception: gives all the work to the imagery, dismissing the prose

options.text: It is not a list, since each movement depends on the one before and the close resolves what the middle raised.

questions.explanation: The three movements form an argument in which each stage depends on the last, and the close solves the problem the middle raises. Calling them a list of reasons misses the necessity of the sequence.
questions.hint: Each stage depends on the one before it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dryden's Fables and the Chaucer couplets inside them
questions.learningObjective: Contrast the older tales with their retellings
questions.stem: The revision handout contrasts the older tales with their retellings. Which contrast is most accurate?

options.text: The retellings elevate the manner and moderate the subject, so both tone and what is permitted change.
The retellings are more explicit in their bawdry, because the new verse form has more room for it.
options.misconception: has the direction of change backwards

options.text: The retellings keep every detail intact, so the older versions can be reconstructed from them.
options.misconception: assumes a retelling leaves nothing out

options.text: The retellings discard the older poems entirely, so no relation between them survives.
options.misconception: denies the visible source relation the collection proclaims

questions.explanation: Recasting into a more elevated verse form changes the manner and what the material can say, since the older tales contain matter the couplet resists.
questions.hint: The manner rises and the subject is moderated.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two different poems both addressed to Celia
questions.learningObjective: Compare the tone of the two poems addressed to Celia
questions.stem: Asked about the tone of the two poems addressed to Celia, the group should say what?

answer.exemplar: One carries its case in a light and elegant register, in which the addressee's own character does most of the work, while the other presses its point in a sustained argument with a sharp turn and a firm closing redefinition. The difference in manner matters as much as the difference in subject, because a reader who has met one poem will expect the other's tone as well as its argument. That expectation is the practical reason for setting them side by side rather than allowing the more famous of the two to stand in for both.

questions.explanation: The answer must identify the difference in manner as well as in argument, since the expectation is the practical point. Shared address does not produce a shared tone.
questions.hint: Compare the manners as well as the arguments.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The two states of The Rape of the Lock
questions.learningObjective: Press a group agreement about the two states for its criterion
questions.stem: In the plenary, students agree that the expanded mock-epic is better. Which response should the tutor give?

options.text: The tutor should agree, since the longer version is generally the more accomplished performance.
options.misconception: accepts an evaluative verdict with no criterion given

options.text: The tutor should ask what question the agreement answers, since longer and better are not the same measure.
The tutor should agree, since the added scenes are generally judged the strongest work in the collection.
options.misconception: invents a consensus about the added scenes

options.text: The tutor should note that the shorter version is the only one a careful reader should ever take seriously.
options.misconception: replaces one dogma with another about which version counts

questions.explanation: The agreement is about length and reputation, not the quality of two artistic solutions, and a tutorial would press the group to say what each version does well. Two published states are two answers.
questions.hint: Ask what the agreement is actually measuring.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Marvell's To His Coy Mistress and its posthumous printing
questions.learningObjective: Refute a claim that early circulation was private

stimulus.body: A handout in the group folder states that the poem was printed only after the poet's death, and that before that it had been copied by hand and set to music. One member asks whether that means the poem was written for private circulation only.

questions.stem: The member's question is put to the group, which must answer it. Which answer is best?

options.text: Yes, because manuscript circulation is by its nature private and cannot be anything else.
options.misconception: assumes manuscript circulation excludes a wider public

options.text: Yes, because songs and manuscripts never reach people beyond a writer's own circle.
options.misconception: denies that manuscript and song can spread a poem widely

options.text: Yes, because the printed volume contained pieces by other writers, so it was a private album.
options.misconception: misreads a printed miscellaneous volume as a keepsake

options.text: No, because manuscript and song circulation made the poem widely known in a way print then regularised.

questions.explanation: Hand copying and song settings carried the poem beyond one circle, and the printed volume gave a stable form to something already known. The early history is wide circulation, not private keeping.
questions.hint: Manuscript and song spread it widely before print.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Temple, 1633, and the machinery that put it in print
questions.learningObjective: Summarise the 1633 collection as a gathering and a made object
questions.stem: At the close of revision, the group writes a summary paragraph on the 1633 collection. Write the paragraph.

answer.exemplar: The 1633 collection is worth studying as both a gathering of poems and a made object. A compiler chose which poems to include and in what order, and a university press then set the volume, choosing type, ruling short lines and dividing the poems for the page, so that the printed book differs in places from the arrangement the poems had known before. Those differences are not errors to be corrected but evidence about how the collection was made, and they explain why its typography, its groupings and its reflowed lines are discussed as evidence in their own right, alongside the poems the book carries.

questions.explanation: The paragraph must present the book as both a gathering and a manufactured object, with the differences treated as evidence. Describing only the poems or only the printing loses the connection.
questions.hint: Gathering and making, with the differences as evidence.
